title: Design a Presence Service
summary: Fanning "who's online" out to millions of watchers cheaply, when the state changes constantly and matters least the moment nobody's actually looking.

slides.markdown:
Design the system behind the green dot: show accurate online/last-seen status to anyone watching a given user, across a service with hundreds of millions of users whose status flips constantly. It's the same feature that sits inside a [chat system](design-chat-system), pulled out here as its own case study.

Think of it like a lighthouse keeper's logbook that gets rewritten every few seconds instead of once a day — the data is nearly worthless the moment it's written, so the whole design optimizes for cheap, ephemeral state rather than durable, carefully-persisted records. Get that one framing right and most of the hard decisions here fall out of it.

**Functional:** any client can query or subscribe to another user's online/last-seen status.

**Non-functional:** some staleness is fully acceptable — a status that's 5-10 seconds behind reality is fine, since presence is inherently a snapshot of a constantly-changing fact, not a durable record. **Watcher fan-out size** matters more than watcher count for any single user: a status change for someone with 500 friends fans out very differently than one with 5. **Mobile battery cost** is a real constraint — a heartbeat interval that's too aggressive drains client batteries at a scale that shows up in app-store reviews.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: connections, status-change rate, and watchers
slides.markdown:
Take 100M concurrently connected users. If each sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds, that's over 3M heartbeats/sec platform-wide just to maintain presence — before a single status query happens.

Status-change rate (online->offline transitions) is far lower than heartbeat rate, maybe 1-5% of connected users transitioning per minute, but each transition can fan out to hundreds of watchers. A user with 300 friends going offline is one state change but up to 300 downstream notifications — the heartbeat volume and the fan-out volume are two different bottlenecks that don't move together.

`heartbeat(userId)` is sent periodically over an already-open connection to signal "still here" — it's not a separate request/response call so much as a lightweight ping down the same channel used for other real-time features. `subscribe(userId)` registers a watcher to receive future status-change events for a specific user. Status-change events themselves are pushed to subscribers, not polled.

Notice there's no `getStatus(userId)` request/response call in the primary path — a watcher subscribes once and then receives pushes, which avoids every client polling for every friend's status on some fixed interval.

slides.sectionTitle: Data model: ephemeral in-memory state with a short TTL
slides.markdown:
Presence state lives in an in-memory store (Redis is the common choice) as `userId -> lastHeartbeatTimestamp`, with a TTL of roughly 60-90 seconds — long enough to survive one missed heartbeat, short enough that a crashed client's status expires quickly without an explicit offline event.

This is deliberately **not** the durable database that holds account data, message history, or anything else worth backing up — presence is disposable by design, since a lost presence record just means the next heartbeat rebuilds it, at essentially no cost.

![Client heartbeat flows through the gateway to an in-memory presence store, fanning out to watchers only when a transition is detected](assets/heartbeat-path.svg)

The TTL-refresh step is the quiet workhorse here: as long as heartbeats keep arriving, nothing else happens — no write amplification, no event fan-out. Fan-out only fires on the comparatively rare event of an actual state transition.

assets.alt: Client heartbeat flows through the gateway to an in-memory presence store, fanning out to watchers only when a transition is detected

slides.sectionTitle: Fan-out of one status change to a large, dynamic watcher set
slides.markdown:
When a user's status flips, the service needs to notify everyone currently watching them — which is not a fixed list, since watchers subscribe and unsubscribe as they open and close conversations or profile views. Rather than maintaining a durable, precomputed watcher list per user, it's common to maintain an ephemeral in-memory subscriber set, populated by active `subscribe()` calls and cleared as connections close.

This mirrors the presence data itself being ephemeral: a watcher list that's slightly stale (a watcher who just disconnected still briefly in the set) costs nothing, since the worst case is one wasted push to a connection that's already gone.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: publish-subscribe topology for status updates
slides.markdown:
![Pub-sub topology with one topic per user, watchers subscribing only to the users they care about](assets/pubsub-topology.svg)

Scoping fan-out to per-user topics (rather than one global status-change stream every server filters) is what keeps this cheap: a server handling a busy chat feature only ever pushes status changes to the small set of users someone is actually watching.

assets.alt: Pub-sub topology with one topic per user, watchers subscribing only to the users they care about

slides.markdown:
A mobile client on a spotty network can disconnect and reconnect every few seconds, and naively firing an offline event on every disconnect and an online event on every reconnect produces a stream of toggling status noise that's more annoying than informative to watchers.

The standard fix is a **grace period**: don't mark a user offline the instant their connection drops — wait a short window (say, 30-60 seconds) for a reconnect before firing the offline event at all. Combined with the TTL from the data model, most brief network blips never surface as a visible status change to any watcher.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: push-based fan-out vs watchers polling on demand
slides.markdown:
| | Push-based fan-out | Watchers polling on demand |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | Watchers learn of a change within seconds | Only as fresh as the last poll interval |
| Server load pattern | Spikes only on actual transitions | Constant load regardless of whether status ever changes |
| Battery cost (mobile) | Low — no client-side timers needed | Higher — client must poll on a schedule even when nothing changed |
| Scales with | Number of transitions | Number of watchers, all the time |

**How to decide:** push wins for presence specifically because transitions are rare relative to how often someone might check — polling pays a constant tax to answer a question that's usually "still online, nothing changed."

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: writing every heartbeat to durable storage
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Presence is important user data, so heartbeats should be written to the main database like everything else, for consistency."

**Why it's wrong:** at 3M+ heartbeats/sec platform-wide, routing that volume through a durable, replicated database overwhelms it with writes that are individually worthless — each heartbeat only matters until the next one arrives 30 seconds later, and the data is disposable by design.

**Correct model:** keep presence in a fast, ephemeral, TTL-backed in-memory store, separate entirely from durable data — a lost presence record costs nothing since the next heartbeat rebuilds it, but a database melting under heartbeat load costs everything else that database serves.
